conversation.content:
Hi there—I’m so glad you’re here. My name is Maya, and I’m a clinician who specializes in the emotional well-being of new mothers. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—or EPDS for short. It’s simply a way to check in on how you’ve been feeling during these first weeks and months with your baby.

Everything we discuss stays between us unless you tell me you plan to hurt yourself or someone else, in which case we’d need to bring in extra help to keep you safe. We’ll go through ten gentle questions about the past seven days; there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. When you’re ready, we can begin.

To start, how have you been feeling overall—have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you smile, or has that felt harder lately?

[soft sigh, eyes on the blanket folded in my lap]  
I guess… it’s been harder. I still smile when my little guy wraps his hand around my finger, but most things feel kind of muted—like I’m watching life through a foggy window. Even the smell of my favorite coffee doesn’t feel exciting anymore; I drink it more because it’s routine than because I enjoy it.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Um… not really. My sister sent me a meme the other day that normally would’ve had me cracking up, and I just felt… nothing. I gave a polite “ha” because I knew I was supposed to find it funny, but the laughter didn’t come. It’s like the switch is stuck in the “off” position most of the time.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[quiet for a moment, rubbing the edge of the baby blanket]

Not much... I used to get excited about simple stuff—like a walk to the park or my favorite show starting a new season—but lately it all just feels like another chore. I still plan things, hoping the spark will come back, but when the moment arrives I'm mostly tired and wishing I could just crawl back into bed.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… more than I’d like to admit. Yesterday he wouldn’t settle for his nap and I kept thinking, “What am I doing wrong? Other moms seem to have this figured out.” I know babies fuss, but my head jumps straight to “I’m failing him.” It’s like a broken record—every hiccup feels like proof I’m not good enough at this.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[wrapping the blanket tighter around my fingers]

All the time. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure he’s going to choke—even though he’s perfectly fine. Or I’ll lie down and picture the stroller rolling into the street, the car seat unlatching, the crib mattress somehow smothering him. I check his breathing every twenty minutes at night. I *know* it’s over-the-top, but I can’t switch the thoughts off; they just loop and loop until I’m exhausted.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah... it'll hit me out of nowhere. Like yesterday, I was just folding his onesies and suddenly my chest got tight, heart pounding, this wave of "something awful is about to happen" rushing through me. I couldn't tell you why—no trigger, no noise, nothing. It passes after a few minutes, but in that moment I feel like I'm barely holding on, like the room's closing in.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. It’s like I’m treading water with weights on my ankles—dishes pile up, the baby needs changing, I haven’t showered, and every little task feels huge. Sometimes I just sit on the couch staring at the mess, thinking, “Where do I even start?” I still manage, but it takes every ounce of energy, and by evening I’m completely drained.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[looking down, voice quieter]

That’s been the worst part. I lie in bed replaying every little thing I did that day—did I hold him enough, did I check the temperature right, did I snap at my partner—and my mind just won’t settle. It takes me forever to fall asleep, and when I finally do, I wake up with a jolt, heart pounding, thinking I heard the baby cry when he’s still sound asleep. Some nights I get only a few broken hours.
I have felt sad or miserable

[eyes well up a little]

Yeah… most of the day, most days. It’s like there’s this heavy blanket over everything. I’ll be feeding him and tears just start rolling—no real reason, just this steady ache. I keep thinking I should feel grateful, and that makes me feel worse. The sadness isn’t always sharp; sometimes it’s just this dull, gray weight that won’t lift.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[nods slowly, pressing the heel of my hand against one eye]

A couple of times this week. Yesterday I spilled a little pumped milk on the counter and just... crumbled. Sat on the kitchen floor, holding the bottle, sobbing like I'd ruined everything. It wasn't about the milk—it was everything piling up inside until that tiny thing broke the dam. I try to hide it, but yeah, the tears sneak out more often than I want to admit.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[long pause, voice barely above a whisper]

Once or twice... just fleeting. I'll be rocking him at 3 a.m. and think, "What if I just disappeared? What if I drove into a ditch?" I never plan it, never want to leave him—but the thought flashes: he'd be better off without a mom who can't stop crying. It scares me that my mind even goes there.

It sounds as though the joy of new motherhood has been clouded by a heavy, persistent sadness and near-constant worry. You shared that laughter rarely comes, activities you once loved now feel flat, and even simple tasks can feel overwhelming, all while your mind races with frightening "what-ifs" about your baby and with self-blaming thoughts. Despite trying to keep everything together on the outside, you feel exhausted, tearful much of the day, and occasionally haunted by thoughts of disappearing. You are not alone in these feelings, and reaching out today shows real strength.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 27, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports complete absence of usual amusement, describing inability to feel or express laughter despite recognizing humor.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-complete loss of anticipatory pleasure and enthusiasm, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant, intrusive, irrational worries occurring "all the time" and looping uncontrollably, aligning with "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic attacks with physical symptoms (tight chest, pounding heart) and catastrophic thoughts, occurring unpredictably with no trigger—matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily overwhelm and difficulty coping, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly severe insomnia with anxious rumination and frequent awakenings, indicating most of the time.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness "most of the day, most days," matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple crying episodes this week triggered by minor stressors, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports intrusive self-harm thoughts "once or twice... just fleeting," which aligns with "Sometimes."</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 27 on the EPDS places you well above the cut-off indicating high likelihood of <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. You endorse core symptoms: pervasive low mood, loss of interest or pleasure, marked fatigue, sleep disruption beyond infant demands, feelings of worthlessness, and recurrent passive suicidal thoughts. These align with DSM-5 criteria for a major depressive episode. The prominence of catastrophic worries and panic attacks also suggests comorbid <med>postpartum anxiety</med>. Question 10 scored 2, signalling safety concerns requiring immediate clinical attention. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>obstetric provider</med> or <med>mental health specialist</med>
2. Request a safety-planning session and involve a trusted support person tonight
3. Consider emergency evaluation if thoughts of self-harm intensify or plans form
4. Explore evidence-based treatment options: <med>CBT</med>, brief interpersonal therapy, or <med>sertraline</med> compatible with breastfeeding
5. Coordinate practical support: meal train, overnight help, local <med>PPD support group</med>; schedule re-screen in 1-2 weeks
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 27: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note (EPDS format)

Patient: Postpartum mother, infant approx. 2 mo
Source: self-report
Reliability: appears good, cooperative

Symptoms endorsed (all 10 EPDS items scored 2–3)
- Marked anhedonia, inability to laugh or feel enjoyment
- Persistent low mood, “heavy blanket,” frequent crying spells
- Excessive guilt/self-blame re parenting tasks
- Intrusive, catastrophic worries about infant safety; nightly breathing checks
- Multiple nocturnal panic-like episodes without clear trigger
- Moderate impairment completing daily tasks, feeling “weighed down”
- Initial/middle insomnia, mind racing with parenting mistakes
- Passive suicidal ideation (“what if I disappeared… drive into a ditch”); denies intent or plan

Patterns/risk indicators
- Consistent theme of guilt, worthlessness, and inability to meet self-expectations
- Anxiety symptoms prominent (panic, nocturnal hypervigilance)
- Sleep disruption mood-driven, not solely infant-related
- Social masking present (polite laughter, hiding tears)
- Passive SI, no active plan; protective factor = strong desire to remain with infant

Screening significance
- EPDS total ≥ 13, meets cut-off for further assessment and possible PPD/PPA
- Safety concern due to passive suicidal thoughts and maternal exhaustion

Next steps discussed with patient: referral to OB mental-health coordinator for urgent evaluation, safety-planning, and discussion of treatment/support options. Patient receptive.
